1.speaker: Brother Juniper
1.text: At noon that day, I was approaching the bridge. The road beneath my feet was white with heat, and five people had already stepped onto the planks. Then the bridge, like a string held taut too long, snapped into the gorge. I stood so close to them, and yet I was still alive. Had they merely arrived a few moments before me?

1.speaker: Brother Juniper
1.text: I believe there is an order to the world. But believing is one thing; facing five deaths is another. I wanted to know how they had lived, whom they had known, whom they had loved. If I could discover all this, might I also understand why it had been these five?

1.speaker: Brother Juniper
1.text: First, someone told me that the old woman who died was very strange. Some remembered her drinking, others her learning. Others still remembered how a letter from Spain could make her seem a different person. I heard many accounts of the same woman that scarcely resembled one another.

1.speaker: Brother Juniper
1.text: Her daughter lived across the sea; beside her lived a girl without parents. Both had letters they wished to write, things they could not say. I would begin with that house, and listen for voices that had never reached the street. Can someone’s hunger for love exhaust the very people who love them?

2.speaker: Esteban
2.text: People in the city were always mistaking us for one another. They would laugh, try the other name, and we would go on with our work. Explaining was tiring; sometimes it was easier to let them talk. As long as my brother stood beside me, I knew their mistakes had not really made either of us disappear.

2.speaker: Esteban
2.text: We scrubbed church walls, copied plays for the theatre, and carried cargo at the shore. At the end of a day, neither had to tell the whole story for the other to know why he was tired. Sometimes we walked the same road separately, so that people would not stop to make jokes again.

2.speaker: Esteban
2.text: Later, he kept going past the theatre and came home later than before. I waited at the table while the candle grew shorter. The life I had thought complete could evidently make room for someone else. I did not understand the change, or know how to ask him about it without sounding accusing.

2.speaker: Esteban
2.text: Later still, someone asked which one I was. I understood perfectly, but gave the other name. Once the answer left my mouth, people were still waiting for me to move on. Standing alone where two people used to live, how can a person know where to go next?

3.speaker: Camila
3.text: The first time I slept in that little bed, I was not thinking of fame. There was hot soup. I was no longer locked up. Someone was teaching me to sing. That alone meant my life had changed. Later, everyone remembered me on the stage; hardly anyone asked about the little girl who had come out of the café.

3.speaker: Camila
3.text: He taught me to understand a line, to turn, to let my voice pause in just the right place. The warmer the audience became, the more I dreaded returning to my dressing room and finding him whistling in a corner. It was as though everyone else’s approval together could not buy one reassuring word from him.

3.speaker: Camila
3.text: I thought of leaving the stage, becoming a respectable woman, being a mother to my children. But each new life I entered was followed by someone calling me by an old name. Even if he had helped me, even if I had once been deeply grateful, that did not mean every door could forever be opened without knocking.

3.speaker: Camila
3.text: Now he has come again, asking to take my child into the city for a year. He says he can teach him many things. I know he can. I also know how frail my boy is. When someone wishes to offer care, should they not pause to hear the answer of the person they would care for?

ending.title: Still Among the Living

segments.text: All five who stepped onto the bridge came from somewhere, and all had things left undone. A letter remained across the sea. A voyage had not begun. Rooms in the city were waiting to be put in order. When the bridge broke, these unfinished things did not become an explanation for the disaster.

Brother Juniper investigated for six years. He recorded every detail he heard, afraid that one omitted fact might mean a lost answer. The cook remembered what María ate; the bookseller spoke of her learning; others remembered an eccentric, tiresome woman. Even those closest to the dead had things they could not put into words.

Earlier, during a plague, he had made a table of fifteen people who died and fifteen who survived, comparing their goodness, piety, and usefulness to their families. The results did not support the explanation he expected. He tore up the paper and cast it into the sea, then recovered his faith from the beauty of sea and sky. That table had never concerned the five people on the bridge.

At last his book about the bridge was finished. It was condemned as heresy, to be burned together with its author. On his last night, the friar still wondered where the plan for his own life lay. At least one wish was clear: he hoped someone would believe that he had begun his inquiry for the sake of faith. In the square, some people did believe him.

Now look back six years, to the memorial service after the collapse. Black veils, candles, silver, and singing filled the church. The captain stayed only a little while, then went down to the sea. Sitting among the girls, the abbess thought of Pepita. She admitted that she had been too busy, and had placed too many hopes for her work upon that child.

Camila had meant to attend as well. On the way, thinking of the crowd, the ceremony, and the faces already growing indistinct, she stopped in a little church. She thought she could feel nothing. Then anguish came: she could never tell Pio that she loved him, never give Jaime fresh courage when he was suffering. She returned to her villa.

A year later, she heard that the abbess had lost two people close to her in the same accident. At first she hid near the convent, watching that plain face. At last she went inside and confessed that she was the former actress. Before she could finish speaking, she bent beneath her grief.

segments.speaker: Camila
segments.text: Mother, what shall I do? I am all alone. I have nothing. I loved them. What shall I do?

The abbess did not immediately offer an explanation. She led Camila into the garden, sent for water, spoke of the nun who tended the flowers, and then asked about the child and friend she had lost. The grief Camila had carried for years had finally found somewhere to rest, without a defense or a performance.

Later, Clara came from Spain, bringing her mother’s last letter to the convent. She struggled to defend her mother, and blamed herself. Reading the letter, the abbess was astonished that such generous sentences had come from someone she had once dismissed. She asked the daughter to stay and see their daily work.

The sun went down, and lamps lit corridor after corridor. Old people, children, the sick, and the blind were here. The abbess still wanted to know whether someone could devise a language for the deaf, whether there were gentler ways of caring for people whose minds were troubled. She was old, yet still asking what could be done next.

Camila was now among her helpers, about to go on an errand across the city. The abbess must still say a few words in the sickroom, then bargain with the flour merchant who was growing impatient. The lamp was set on the floor. The patients looked at her. Outside it was dark; inside, someone stayed to offer a little light and warmth.

The abbess thought that, in time, even those who remembered the five would die. Those who had loved them would be loved a little longer, and would also be forgotten. Yet the love had existed. The heart’s reaching toward another did not depend upon being remembered forever.

segments.speaker: Mother Pilar’s thoughts
segments.text: There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning.

ending.credit: Adapted from Thornton Wilder’s The Bridge of San Luis Rey, published in 1927 and awarded the 1928 Pulitzer Prize for the Novel. Interior voices and scenes are abridged or reconstructed. The final sentence follows the original English.

cards.title: The Weight of Jewels

segments.text: [[NPC1]]'s father made his fortune in cloth, and earned his neighbours' dislike along with it. Their house stood near the great square, but that did not make it easier for his daughter to enter the life of the city. She stammered and was not considered pretty. Her mother was determined to make her sociable; the less progress she saw, the sharper her ridicule became.

Before they went out, her mother hung {{e_jewels|Jewels}} upon her, one piece after another. Gold and silver could not speak for her. They served instead as a conspicuous harness, exposing every shrinking movement to the room. She lived alone with her thoughts. Suitors began to call; what they saw in her fortune was easier to explain than what they saw in her.

She insisted that she would never marry. Mother and daughter quarrelled, accused each other, slammed doors. She believed that if she held her ground on this one matter, some part of her life might remain her own. Her resistance lasted until she was twenty-six. It ended in marriage to an impoverished, haughty nobleman.

At the wedding the church was full of the guests' whispered mockery. The cloth merchant's money had purchased a title, but the title could not shield her from their looks. In time she had a great house and servants, and people were obliged to address her formally as the Marquesa. Only the habit of sitting alone, waiting for someone to want her company, survived the change in rank.

Years later she placed all her hopes upon another little girl. The child's name was {{e_clara|Clara}}, and her beauty seemed almost unbelievable. At last there was someone she could love without reserve. She had not yet learned how to let that person grow freely.

cards.title: The Murmurs at the Wedding

segments.text: I can hear them. The church in {{e_lima|Lima}} is so large, and so many people are speaking softly. Every word seems far away and right against my ear. If I do not look up, I need not discover whose face is laughing. I have put on the clothes they wanted me to wear and married the man they were willing to accept. Why have I still not done it right?

Mother dislikes the way I speak. When I am nervous, a word has to strike against my mouth several times before it comes out. People have already begun to feel impatient, or embarrassed for me. Yet alone I have so much to say. Without interruptions I can think a thing through, even invent a remark that might make someone laugh. When I sit before them, the remark is gone.

Once I thought I would never marry. With the door shut, it still seemed possible. When the door opened again, the accounts, the relations and the suitors were all waiting outside. I did not know quite whom they were waiting for.

These {{e_jewels|Jewels}} are still here. They attract attention more easily than my words. How I wish that one day someone would come to my side simply because they wanted to sit with me for a while. I would never let that person feel lonely again. They call me señora. I still do not know how to lift my head.

cards.title: A Correction at Eight

segments.text: By the time [[NPC2]] was eight, she could calmly correct her mother's choice of words. She resembled her father: clever, composed, able to watch another person's agitation without sharing it. [[NPC1]], meanwhile, grew increasingly afraid of her daughter's startled looks. She tried to be gentle, tried to please, watched for every need—and invariably offered the thing before the child had wanted it.

Such attentions were difficult to refuse. Reject one small favour and it seemed that you had rejected all the love behind it; accept reluctantly, and the next enquiry followed. The daughter grew weary, the mother alarmed. After an argument two doors closed, and the same house suddenly became enormous. Sitting alone, the mother rehearsed their conversation over and over, searching each time for a sentence that might bring her daughter back.

People would later call this daughter heartless. Yet as an adult she generously helped friends, servants and gifted strangers, tending to them as if they were her children. Her coldness was not bestowed equally upon everyone. Before the one person who most longed for her tenderness, she felt she must first defend a little distance.

More proposals arrived. The mother imagined someone joining their life; the daughter considered how to leave it. The marriage she finally chose required her to settle in {{e_spain|Spain}}. It was not the next street. A letter sent there might wait half a year for an answer.

Little by little the luggage was packed. The doors that had once closed after quarrels would stand open after the daughter left. Her mother could add another possession to a trunk, ask whether something might be needed on the journey. None of these small errands could abolish the sea already lying between them.

cards.cgPrompt: An intelligent eight-year-old girl in a pale colonial dress corrects her anxious mother's speech across a sitting room table; the mother's affectionate hands hesitate in midair; high windows, early morning, intimate distance.

cards.title: No Answer Behind the Door

segments.text: {{e_clara|Clara}} has shut the door again. I know I should not go to it at once. Asking through the wood whether she is angry will only make her angrier. But if I never ask, how will she know I am waiting?

I am not angry when she corrects me. She is so clever; I ought to be pleased. I am only a little afraid. Once I have said something wrong, whatever follows seems to require her permission. So I talk still more, explaining a small matter at great length, until the weariness I most dread appears on her face.

As a child I feared a door suddenly opening too: Mother coming in to ask why I was standing like that again, why I could not be like other girls. How have I made my own child want to escape her room? Surely what I give her ought to be different from what I received.

If she would come out and say she did not blame me, I could be quiet. She need not even say it. She could sit beside me. {{e_loneliness|Loneliness}} was mine alone, yet I keep requiring an answer from her before I can believe that today may pass. I listen to the sounds behind her door. Even I can see that this waiting must distress her. When the room grows quiet, I am more frightened still.

cards.cgPrompt: A worried middle-aged mother seated outside her daughter's closed carved wooden door in a colonial mansion, an unused cup on a small tray, warm light stopping at the threshold, no child visible.

cards.title: A Hymn Across the Water

segments.text: Before the ship sailed, a blessing was given. For so distant a journey, embraces and waving could not be enough: people aboard and people ashore knelt together and sang a hymn. The wide sea received their voices without making them stronger. The singing sounded thin, hesitant. Already the water between the hull and the shore was widening.

[[NPC1]] was perfectly composed. She had chosen a marriage that would take her to {{e_spain|Spain}}, and was moving towards the life she had chosen. Behind her, her mother stood on the shore, pressing a hand now to her heart, now to her mouth, as though the farewell might retain its dignity if only she could keep something from bursting out of her chest.

The sailing ship grew brighter before [[NPC2]]'s eyes, while its outline grew less distinct. Tears streaked the tranquil Pacific. The huge pearl-coloured clouds seemed as if they would remain there forever. People could sail away beneath them, however, to a place where one could not knock on a door at any moment or hear an immediate reply.

The daughter aboard showed none of the distress her mother hoped to see. Composure might mean courage before a voyage, or relief at having at last obtained distance. From the shore, one could not judge by so remote a figure. The mother watched until the ship no longer allowed her to distinguish anyone on its deck.

In time, {{e_letters|Letters between mother and daughter}} would travel between the two continents. Sailing dates would become the measure of her life, and the few sentences her daughter chose to write would be unfolded again and again. No amount of rereading would shorten this water. The ship too had received its blessing. No one had explained to the mother on the shore how to bring this farewell to an end.

cards.cgPrompt: A colonial sailing ship just leaving the Peruvian Pacific shore, mother on the quay pressing one hand to her mouth, daughter composed on deck, kneeling figures singing, vast pearly clouds dwarfing both groups.

cards.title: The Door She Kissed

segments.text: Four years have passed since we last parted. On the voyage here I told myself: do not rush towards her, do not weep, do not lay all those years of words upon {{e_clara|Clara}} at once. To live in the same house as her is already enough.

She tried too. We both knew that some things should never have been said. This time, if I asked a little less and she was a little more patient, perhaps we could sit down to a peaceful meal. Before it was over I heard my voice change. She put down what she was holding. We had returned to the moment we knew best.

Dawn has not yet come in {{e_spain|Spain}}. She sleeps behind the door; I stand outside it. If I wake her, there will be another farewell, more explanations, more tears over words I had meant to say lightly. Let her sleep. I press my lips to the door, just once. It does not open. This time I do not knock.

When I am home again, paper will be quieter than I am. A mistaken sentence can be crossed out; an urgent one rewritten. She need not watch me struggle to speak, and I need not see at once where she has grown tired of reading. Tomorrow must still be lived. The ship will not wait until I have finally learned to say goodbye.

cards.cgPrompt: Before dawn in a Spanish house, a visiting older Peruvian mother lightly kisses the closed door behind which her adult daughter sleeps, a small travel bag at her feet, blue window light and a dying candle.

cards.title: Before the Mail Sails

segments.text: As the mailing day approached, [[NPC1]] ventured out again. She endured dinners and looks in the street, listened to strange events at the {{e_court|Viceroy’s palace}}, read {{e_scripts|Copied plays}}, and sought a story or two for her {{e_letters|Letters between mother and daughter}}. She did not lack money or expect these compositions to win her fame. She wanted her daughter to smile suddenly as she read. She followed celebrated people such as {{e_camila|Camila}}, remembering the actress's reputation at the {{e_theatre|Lima’s theatre}}.

{{e_clara|Clara}} had written that the king admired her {{e_goldchain|Gold chain}} and asked her mother to send a similar one as soon as possible. Her mother turned the purchase into an adventure: at midnight she climbed into a painting, the painter reached through the colours to help her, and she explained to its inhabitants that the loveliest girl in the world wished to present a gift to the most courteous king. It was a joke in a letter. The only surface she could truly cross remained a sheet of paper.

She wrote of her daughter's cold, of the gum sold by the nuns. After solemn advice she could not resist adding a sharp observation. Anxiety and wit sat side by side, like the two things she wanted to say: take good care of yourself; and spare another glance for your mother. As the night deepened she rearranged her sentences until the heavy wish appeared light.

Before dawn, the envelope and presents were wrapped together to await the shipping agent. Once the letter left her hands, she often retreated into drink and sleep until the next mailing day drew near. The letters were chiefly preserved by her son-in-law, who admired their style. Her daughter generally glanced through them.

Many years later, students would study these sentences and scholars would debate the making of her style. The woman at the desk was not looking so far ahead. She merely folded the paper, hoping that this time there might be some echo from across the sea.

cards.cgPrompt: A red-wigged aging noblewoman rewrites a letter late at night at a carved wooden desk, discarded drafts, a small gold chain and wax sealing tools, first light entering a green balcony, no legible writing.

cards.title: The Green Balcony

segments.text: I wonder whether something here in my chest has truly gone wrong. If a physician opened it, could he see the traces of these years? I wrote the thought to {{e_clara|Clara}}. She reproached me for studying only myself and making a god of sorrow.

From the balcony of the {{e_palace|Marquesa’s house}}, it is easy to watch people kissing and greeting one another and suspect that they perform it for an audience. I know the thought is cruel. Still I ask myself: if they have not suffered as I have, what makes their love real?

Then I am afraid to raise my eyes. I want her to love me, and to admit that I am better than other mothers. I wait for her to ask my forgiveness, as though every fault lay on her side. Even the reconciliation I imagine must end with her yielding.

She has placed thousands of miles between us. I have no opportunity left to rule her, yet I am still wrestling with the desire. A page of tenderness does not mean that I can let go. But what else do I know how to do, except write another page?

cards.cgPrompt: An aging red-wigged woman alone on a green wooden colonial balcony, straw hat casting a purple shadow, ringed fingers against her chest and an open letter in her lap, city noise distant below.

cards.title: Beside the Washing Trough

segments.text: [[NPC1]] feared less for her own death than for the sickbeds, orphans and homeless women who would remain after it. Finishing her accounts at night, she often imagined a day when women might organise to protect women travelling alone, women in service, women in mines and workshops. In the morning she still had to go begging for this month's expenses.

She began to look for a successor. Through wards, courtyards and corridors she hurried, inspecting face after face, disappointed by her own haste. At last she stopped beside the washing trough. A twelve-year-old girl was directing the others at their work while telling the miracles of Saint Rose of Lima with tremendous dramatic enthusiasm. That girl was [[NPC2]].

From then on the least popular duties often fell to the girl. On journeys she carried eggs and vegetables; at home she learned how each part of the institution worked. Sometimes, in the middle of a task, the older woman in black would call her aside and discuss the arrangement of contagious wards, the management of people, or how to ask the wealthy for money. These were not merely orders. It was almost as if a colleague were being briefed.

When {{e_maria|María}} came to borrow an orphan as a companion, the abbess saw an opportunity. The girl would encounter the world outside; perhaps the rich old woman could be turned towards useful work. She weighed the strain the arrangement would impose upon the girl and believed she knew when to draw back.

At first the girl visited for occasional afternoons. Eventually she went to live there. Two years of training had taught her many responsibilities. No one had taught her with equal care how to admit that a burden was too much.

cards.cgPrompt: A sturdy elderly abbess in a black veil observes a twelve-year-old orphan girl directing other girls at a stone laundry trough, white linen, sunlight in an austere convent courtyard, the child's animated hand telling a story.

cards.title: Treated as a Grown-Up

segments.text: Sometimes {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} comes to find me without warning. I am still holding the eggs when she begins to talk about the wards, about which two people will quarrel if put together, or whom we should ask for help so the journey will not be wasted. I thought such things ought to be said to other grown-ups. But she keeps looking at me, as if I can understand them too.

I want to remember. Someone is waiting for everything she asks. The sick cannot miss a meal because I am afraid; the roof cannot keep leaking because money is hard to borrow. When I listen to her, those things feel close. Perhaps if I try a little harder, I can become the person she needs.

Back in bed, though, I feel small again. When she asks whether I can manage, of course I say yes. If she knew I sometimes cried in secret, would she think she had mistaken me? At {{e_convent|Convent of Santa Rosa}}, when I do not understand, I can wait for her to come near. How long will I have to wait in that lady's house?

Everyone says I should be glad: it is a sign of trust. I am glad. I simply did not know that trust could weigh so much, or that, unlike a basket, it could not be set on the ground when my arms grew tired. What she wants me to remember goes far beyond today's errands.

cards.cgPrompt: A young orphan girl holding a basket of eggs and vegetables while an elderly abbess discusses hospital arrangements beside a convent corridor, the girl's attentive face carrying pride and apprehension, afternoon light.

cards.title: A Borrowed Place

segments.text: When the mistress remained in bed for days, the servants lent rooms to their relations and took whatever they wanted from the house. Sometimes there was no need even to conceal it. The only person who truly saw what they were doing was a girl in an orphanage uniform.

[[NPC1]] refused to pretend she had seen nothing. So she endured torments that were difficult to name as serious offences: doors locked her in, errands were deliberately complicated. She had to watch for missing possessions while fearing that her mistress would accuse her of taking them. The servants knew the house better than she did. They also knew how far a child without a family to defend her could be pushed.

Occasionally {{e_maria|María}} emerged from her preoccupations and talked to her, revealing wit, insight and warmth. Just as the girl began to feel attached to her, the next day's gaze would pass over her as if she were a familiar piece of furniture. The lady need not lose her temper to spend an entire day without really seeing her.

She remembered the duties {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} had given her. She had been sent as a companion, with no promise that she would be happy. When unhappiness came, she first wondered whether she had done her duty properly. Soft footsteps, quietly closed doors, coming at once when called: all these were easier than explaining why she was hurt.

The great house had room for the servants' relations, chests of presents and portraits of the daughter overseas. After moving in, the girl still could find no one to whom she could safely speak. She finished her work and waited for another day when her mistress might care to talk. She still wore her convent uniform. Her mistress had not thought to provide another dress.

cards.cgPrompt: A fourteen-year-old orphan companion stands alone in a grand colonial mansion hallway while servants secretly carry household goods past a half-open bedroom, her faded uniform contrasting with expensive carved furniture, restrained domestic tension.

cards.title: Stay in the Sun

segments.text: {{e_maria|María}} told me to stay in the sunshine. She would not be long. This stone is still warm, but now the shadow has reached my shoes. I thought of going into the church to look for her. What if she came out and could not find me?

At last I went in. She was not there. I searched the pews, reached another door, and understood that she had probably left by it. May I go home now? Or must I return to the place where she told me to wait? Her instruction was so simple. I have made it harder and harder.

People are always passing through the square in {{e_lima|Lima}}. When I hear lowered voices, I think they are talking about my clothes. Perhaps some have not even looked at me, but I still want to hide the edge of my skirt. Everyone knows this uniform. Everyone knows where I came from.

{{e_obedience|Obedience}} ought to make things clear. Do as you are told and you will disappoint no one. I return to the same corner and stand in the lengthening shadow. If she passes this way once more, she will know that I did not wander off.

cards.cgPrompt: An adolescent girl in a faded orphanage uniform waiting at the edge of a Lima church square, long afternoon shadows stretching toward her, the side church door in the distance empty, passersby blurred without threatening caricature.

cards.title: Laughter Towards the Box

segments.text: During the interval, [[NPC2]] set aside her dignified role and came before the curtain to sing the topical songs popular in the city. She had noticed the old lady in her box. She improvised verses about her looks, her drinking, her stinginess, even her daughter's departure overseas. {{e_pio|Pio}} ordinarily helped her learn her lines and judge a performance. These improvised songs were hers to control.

The audience understood quickly. Eyes turned from the stage to the box, and laughter rose in successive waves. [[NPC1]] was still thinking of the two acts she had just seen, and of {{e_spain|Spain}}. Her attention had wandered far away. A few fine phrases were forming in her mind; perhaps her daughter would like them in a letter.

The singer grew bolder. Beside the lady, [[NPC3]] heard everything. She tugged her sleeve and quietly urged her to leave. She did not rise to argue with the whole theatre; she only wanted to take her mistress beyond those staring eyes. When the two left the box, the audience rose cheering, as though a battle had been won.

The actress broke into a lively dance. Seeing the manager behind the stage, she knew that this triumph would increase her fee. The audience's {{e_applause|Applause}} assured her that today's cruelty had succeeded.

The old lady being led outside was almost pleased. The performance had given her phrases that might amuse her daughter. She did not know that she too had become material for someone else's amusement. In the same uproar, the actress heard approval, the girl heard humiliation, and the lady heard almost nothing. Everyone had looked towards her box. No one had waited for her answer.

cards.cgPrompt: Colonial Lima theatre during an interval song: celebrated actress on a candlelit stage, audience turning toward an upper box where a distracted older noblewoman sits and a young companion quietly tugs her sleeve, cinematic three-plane composition.

cards.title: An Insult Unheard

segments.text: The actress arrived in black, carrying a letter from {{e_viceroy|Viceroy Andrés}}. [[NPC1]] rubbed her forehead with snow, put on her cloak and struggled into the drawing room. [[NPC2]] had prepared a few perfunctory remarks. Now the old lady's bearing unsettled her.
You have come—was there something you wished?
I wanted to be certain that you had not misunderstood what you heard at the theatre that evening. An actress such as myself sometimes says more than she means.
Misunderstood? I remember only how beautifully you acted. You are a great artist. You ought to be happy.
I mean the songs between the acts. I feared you might think I had intended to show you disrespect.
Ah, we left early. Forgive us—right in the middle of your wonderful performance. I forget why. Someone was unwell, perhaps.
The actress blushed. She could not believe that anyone had failed to understand the songs. She could only interpret these words as forgiveness.
You are so good, to forgive my childishness. I did not know before. Please let me kiss your hand.

How could I be angry with you, my beautiful child? One of your gestures reminded me of {{e_clara|Clara}}. Once we quarrelled, then both returned to ask forgiveness, with only a door between us. She took my face in both hands, like this.
Weeping, the lady leaned forward to demonstrate the gesture she had dreamed so often. That reconciliation had never occurred in her waking life.
People in the city say she treats me badly. It is not true. She is intelligent and gracious; I am the difficult one. I weary people when I speak, and yet I became the mother of so beautiful a girl.

She almost fell from the chair. {{e_pepita|Pepita}} steadied her and took her back to her room. At home, the actress stood a long while before her mirror, both hands against her own face. She had not brought back the easy relief she had expected from the apology.

cards.cgPrompt: A famous actress in a plain black dress kneels in confusion beside an aging noblewoman wearing a fur-trimmed cloak indoors, the older woman's hands demonstrating a dreamed embrace, a young orphan at the doorway, quiet late afternoon.

cards.title: Red Chalk on the Stairs

segments.text: The news was almost hidden at the end of the letter. {{e_clara|Clara}} wrote that she could not travel that autumn as planned: her child would be born in early October. She made little of it, hoping to provoke less anxiety in her mother. [[NPC1]] caught hold of the wall. What child? Her daughter was to become a mother?

She began asking questions at once. What did the old women of the city know? Which remedies were said to work? She gathered everything and put it into letters. Details that bored the reader across the sea became her most urgent daily business. The greater the distance and the less she could do, the more she wanted to try every possibility.

There must be no knots in the house; even the maids could not tie their hair tightly. She marked the even-numbered stairs with red chalk. When someone stepped wrongly she wept, shouted and drove them out. She concealed protective charms on her body, as though one oversight might harm the life about to begin across the sea.

Before daybreak she went to the earliest Mass. Gripping the altar rail, she gazed at the sacred images and begged for the slightest nod. Yet after a day of such exertion she sometimes felt that nature was deaf and God indifferent. Nothing she did had touched the course of events.

The despair never lasted. As soon as a new 'perhaps' arose, she hurried home to replace the candles. At last she decided to make a pilgrimage to the {{e_shrine|Shrine of Cluxambuqua}}. Her chair would cross the {{e_bridge|Bridge of San Luis Rey}} and climb into the Andes. She hoped the ancient shrine might offer a firmer assurance than the markings in her house. She performed every observance earnestly, with ever less certainty that she could still protect her daughter.

cards.cgPrompt: An anxious older noblewoman marks alternating stair steps with red chalk in her colonial house; a maid stands with loosened hair, candles before a distant portrait, superstitious domestic arrangements, no supernatural effects.

cards.title: Make the Room Ready

segments.text: {{e_maria|María}} went straight to the shrine without getting out of her chair at the door. She has left this place to me. By the time she returns, it must at least be a room one can live in. The porters are waiting. I show them which basket goes by the wall and which must be opened first.

The altar, tapestries and portraits of her daughter all have to come out. This room at the {{e_inn|Mountain inn}} is not the room at home. If the arrangement feels strange, she may be unable to settle. It is cold here; the brazier must be prepared. I must go downstairs and tell the cook how to make the {{e_porridge|Porridge}}. I cannot be vague about that. It is mostly what she manages to eat.

The mountain air makes me dizzy. I press my hand against the table and wait for it to pass, thinking of what remains undone. As long as I do one thing after another, there is no time to think how far away the {{e_convent|Convent of Santa Rosa}} has become.

At last the room is ready, but there are still no footsteps outside. With nothing to do, familiar voices return: advice at supper, prayers beside the sickbeds, the abbess asking me to stay and talk. I take out paper, then lay down the quill. A letter should not delay my work very much. At least there will be hot porridge to her liking when she comes back.

cards.cgPrompt: A young companion unpacks wicker hampers in a modest Andean inn, arranging a small household altar and a framed portrait while a brazier waits on the stone floor; cold mountain sunlight, sleeves rolled with practical care.

cards.title: A Letter by the Fountain

segments.text: When the white-walled mountain town came into view, [[NPC1]]'s fingers stopped moving over her rosary. The Andes rose so high that the town seemed to rest upon their knees. Bells answered one another. In the clear cold air her hurried prayers suddenly ceased to tumble out in succession.

At the shrine an attendant demanded an obscure fee, then asked her to move on the pretext of repairing the floor. Elsewhere this might have disturbed her. Today she changed places and remained seated. The old candle-sellers talked of money all day; even they did not interrupt her. Dimly she felt that perhaps her daughter's life and the affairs of God did not need her constant urging.

Later she sat beside the fountain, watching the sick move slowly around the garden and three hawks circle above. A thick-fleeced llama approached, bringing its soft nose near as though it too wished to join a conversation. Others followed, gathering round this woman who was no longer in a hurry.

A messenger boy found her. She had ordered that any news from {{e_spain|Spain}} be brought immediately. She opened the packet, first reading her son-in-law's witty, affectionate note, then {{e_clara|Clara}}'s letter. Her daughter's clever sentences had sharp edges. As each one wounded her, she wrapped it in understanding and forgiveness and laid it in her heart.

This time she did not rush away or send anyone on an errand. She put away the {{e_letters|Letters between mother and daughter}}, rose slowly, gently dispersed the curious llamas and returned to the shrine. The square's bells were still ringing. Her face was grave, but she no longer asked the world what more she must do to obtain assurance. She did not tell the strangers nearby of her daughter's harshness. She kept the letter in her own hands.

cards.cgPrompt: An aging noblewoman on the steps of a mountain town fountain quietly reading a delivered letter, curious llamas close beside her, whitewashed sanctuary and distant Andes, crystalline afternoon air, tenderness without sentimentality.

cards.title: May I Come Back for a Few Days?

segments.text: I only meant to tell {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} that we had safely reached the {{e_inn|Mountain inn}}. Yet the ink spots kept multiplying as I wrote. She is so busy. Will seeing them make her worry about me too?

…None of it matters, so long as you love me and wish me to stay with the lady. I ought not to tell you, but sometimes the wicked maids lock me in my room and take things away. Perhaps the lady will think I have stolen them. I hope not. I hope you are well, and that there is no trouble at the hospital or anywhere else.

Though I cannot see you, I think of you all the time and remember what you have taught me. I only want to do what you wish. But might I come back to the convent for a few days? If you do not wish it, there is no need. I am only so lonely, with no one to talk to, and other things…
Sometimes I do not know whether you have forgotten me. If you could find a little time to write even a very short letter, I could keep it with me. But I know how busy you are…

She put down the quill and left the ink-spotted letter. Downstairs she asked about fresh {{e_charcoal|Charcoal}} and tasted the porridge in the pot. Among these small tasks, her hands once more knew exactly what to do.

cards.cgPrompt: An adolescent girl writes an ink-blotted private letter at a small inn table, lip trembling as she pauses with the quill, an open doorway leading down toward the kitchen, no visible readable lettering.

cards.title: Letter Fifty-Six

segments.text: [[NPC1]] had read the girl's letter on the table. After closing it, she wanted to read it again. She envied the devotion that {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} inspired in a child, and felt ashamed of making love so burdensome herself. The girl brought in supper.
Child, will you not eat with me?
I thought you would be tired. I have eaten downstairs. Shall I read to you while you eat?
No, thank you. Go to bed if you wish. Wait—I am sending a letter to Lima tomorrow morning. If you have one, it can go with mine.
I have none. I must go down and fetch fresh charcoal for you.
But the one to the abbess… I know she would be delighted to receive it.
I am not sending it. I have changed my mind. It was not a good letter.
Why not, my dear? I thought it very beautiful. Believe me, I know about such things. What made it a bad letter?
It was not… not brave.

The girl would say no more. She took the letter into her room. The woman at the table heard paper tearing and looked down at her supper. {{e_courage|Courage}}: she had never seriously brought that word into love. Remembering her demands for answers, she first wanted to defend herself, to blame her upbringing and circumstances. At last she cleared the table and sat down to write again.

This became the fifty-sixth of her celebrated {{e_letters|Letters between mother and daughter}}. She called it her first, as though her appeals could finally take another form. She could not retrieve the old letters that repeatedly asked how much her daughter loved her. This new one could still be more generous. When she finished, dawn was near.

cards.cgPrompt: At a mountain inn supper table, an older noblewoman gently offers to send a young companion's letter; the girl stands by the brazier avoiding her gaze, an untouched bowl of porridge and folded paper between them, intimate candlelit distance.

cards.title: The Paper Never Sent

segments.text: Once I said that word, I wanted to say nothing more. {{e_maria|María}} kept looking at me. She really thought the letter beautiful. I am not used to anyone asking why I will not send it.

Tearing paper makes a loud sound. In such a quiet room at the {{e_inn|Mountain inn}}, it must be audible next door. I tore it smaller, but the things I had written did not disappear. I still want to go back for a few days. I still wish {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} would write me a few words, even a letter small enough to fit in my palm.

After lying down I remember how I spoke, and feel uneasy. I should not have spoken so loudly. Perhaps I should not have called it a bad letter. Now the paper is in pieces, and asking for another sheet would mean explaining everything again. No one questions me in the dark. I am still answering in my head.

Eventually the girl slept. Near dawn, the lady came in holding a candle and gently brushed the damp hair from her forehead. The unsent letter never returned to the mailbag. Two days later they set out for the city, towards the {{e_bridge|Bridge of San Luis Rey}} they had crossed on their way there.

cards.cgPrompt: A young girl awake in a dark small inn bedroom, torn fragments of an unsent letter on the bedside table, the warm light beneath the door hinting at another person still writing; a quiet compassionate image without triumphant mood.

cards.title: The Basket at the Door

segments.text: One morning two boys were found in the basket for abandoned infants at the door. Before the wet-nurse arrived, they already had names: {{e_manuel|Manuel}} and {{e_esteban|Esteban}}. The names were distinct; the children were not. No one in the city could reliably tell which was which.

No one knew their parents. Later, seeing how straight they stood and how silent they were, the city's gossips invented distinguished origins for them, assigning them to one noble doorway after another. None of these stories restored a family to them or spared them any teasing as they grew.

[[NPC1]] was the nearest thing they had to a guardian. She often hated the suffering men brought upon women, yet gradually grew fond of these two children. In the evenings she called them into her room, sent to the kitchen for cakes, and told stories of heroes and the successive misfortunes of a clown.

Two pairs of dark eyes watched her intently. The more she loved them, the more abruptly she would worry: when they became men, would the things she hated emerge from these faces too? The boys did not understand the hesitation in her gaze. They waited for the story to continue.

They remained until they were a little too old to stay, then worked in churches throughout the city: mending hedges, polishing crucifixes, carrying the censer behind priests entering sickrooms. Everyone knew the brothers, and still confused their names. Later they became copyists. With their similar hands they transcribed plays, ballads, merchants' notices and endless parts for the choirs. They had possessed names from the beginning. Only each brother could recognise the other without needing one.

cards.title: Had We Been There

segments.text: When she reached the part where they nailed the man up, I interrupted. If {{e_esteban|Esteban}} and I had been there, we would have stopped them. It did not sound like a boast when I said it. Two people could surely do something. How could they simply stand and watch?

{{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} looked at us for a while. Her stories of distant places often contained people suffering, or people who arrived too late. I disliked hearing 'too late'. When we ran errands for her, a blocked road meant finding another. If something was heavy, we each took one end.

People in the city confuse us, then laugh at their own mistake. I do not want to explain so much. In this room at {{e_convent|Convent of Santa Rosa}}, we can sit beside one another, listen quietly, and speak when we wish.
Had we been there, we would have changed it. When I said that, I had never yet met a thing that had to be done and could not be done, however hard one tried.

cards.title: Words They Would Not Surrender

segments.text: The {{e_archbishop|Archbishop of Lima}} heard that the twins spoke a language only they understood. He trimmed a quill and summoned them to his study. He had studied dialects and hoped to make an interesting project of these materials when he returned to his estate in Spain.
How do you say bread? When you are alone together, what word do you use?
{{e_manuel|Manuel}} and {{e_esteban|Esteban}} stood upon the fine carpet. After a long silence one of them answered softly. Their questioner moved his pen towards the paper.
And a tree? Do you have a word for a tree as well? Do not be troubled. Just say what you ordinarily say.

Another silence. They had possessed this {{e_language|The twins’ private language}} since learning to speak; its vocabulary and syntax owed little to Spanish. They used it when alone. On the rare urgent occasion before others, they whispered.
Then would 'I see' differ from 'I have seen'? Slowly, please, so that I can write it down.

They did not know how to explain why this seemingly harmless business embarrassed them so deeply. They could answer; it was not merely awe of his rank. Strangers usually found amusement in staring at their similar faces. Now, question by question, even the most private space between them was being laid upon the desk.

At first their host thought the splendour of his study had restrained them. Eventually he perceived that their hesitation came from somewhere deeper. Disappointed, he put down the quill and dismissed them without asking for another word. The language remained between the brothers. The notebook held far less than he had expected.

cards.title: The Same Errand

segments.text: People ask why we take different streets even when going on the same errand. It saves us hearing them guess who is who. They laugh when they are right and when they are wrong. Whatever we answer, we have to stand there until they have finished.

{{e_esteban|Esteban}} need not tell me when he will return. Sometimes, at my work, I feel he is almost here. A little later there are footsteps outside. If others heard that, they would probably ask many questions. We are used to it. We do not feel obliged to explain.

When we tire of copying, we carry cargo at the {{e_harbor|Lima’s harbor}}. We have driven animals, picked fruit, ferried people across water. Different work makes different parts of the back ache. At home there is still someone who knows why I am quiet that day.

We seldom discuss anything grand. Food, clothing, where to earn tomorrow's money: a few words suffice. Whether it is two desks or a heavy wooden crate, I know someone is on the other side. However noisy the rest of the world becomes, I need not understand it immediately.

cards.title: The One Who Stayed

segments.text: The manager expected empty seats that evening and gave the brothers two tickets. Since returning to the city they had resumed copying for the company. They went backstage regularly, without finding much to admire in the speeches. Honour, fame, the flames of love: once a poet began, everything could be made to circle those subjects for a very long time.

They sat patiently, watching the candles and splendid clothes. During the interval {{e_camila|Camila}} shed her dramatic role and came out to dance in layered skirts. {{e_esteban|Esteban}} said he had copying to finish and went home. [[NPC1]] remained. The red stockings and shoes never entirely left his thoughts.

They had seen the actress before. Years earlier she had brought them together, inspected their faces carefully, then clapped one on the shoulder and announced that she had found the younger. The embarrassment of that inspection had long sunk beneath other memories. Now one brother found that almost every errand somehow led him towards her house.

At night he stood among the trees beneath her dressing-room window, his knuckles against his mouth, listening to his heartbeat. She was the mistress of {{e_viceroy|Viceroy Andrés}}: rich, beautiful and sharp-tongued. Almost nothing he knew of her offered hope. None of it persuaded him to go home.

His brother waiting in their room also bit his knuckles. He had not fallen in love with the actress. He could not understand why two people, who had always been enough, should suddenly no longer suffice. For the first time the same silence concealed two things they could not immediately understand in each other.

cards.cgPrompt: A quiet dark-haired young copyist remains in a candlelit theatre audience as his identical brother leaves down an aisle, celebrated actress dancing in layered skirts and red shoes beyond the footlights, fascination held in a still face.

cards.title: Writing Another Man's Love

segments.text: At the {{e_theatre|Lima’s theatre}}, {{e_camila|Camila}} said I seemed not to like her. I did not know how to answer like a friend without betraying my delight at being there. I said, 'Yes, señora.' She called me stupid. When I said it again, she threatened to find someone else.

She made me swear that even {{e_esteban|Esteban}} must not know. I kept a secret between us, only to receive words for other men. The letter to {{e_viceroy|Viceroy Andrés}} rebuked his suspicions and returned his presents. The one to the bullfighter became an affectionate arrangement.

The quill did not stop. She told me to take another sheet, and I took one. Not a sentence in these {{e_secretletters|Secret love letters}} was addressed to me. Yet she stood so near that I felt, if I wrote clearly enough, I might stay a little longer.

She asked whether I had copied it correctly and paid me. {{e_pio|Pio}} usually wrote for her, she said, but she did not want him to know of these letters. I took the money, went downstairs and stood beneath the trees. The words I had been obliged to hear so precisely now crowded my heart. I could not find a single word of my own.

cards.title: A Copyist at Midnight

segments.text: There was a light knock. [[NPC2]] rose to open the door, and a veiled woman hurried in, asking first for ink and paper. [[NPC3]] was already in bed, watching from beneath the covers. The visitor noticed his eyes, apologised hastily for coming so late, and leaned over the table.

[[NPC1]] was writing to the bullfighter who had kept her waiting. Close to the copyist's ear she dictated angry sentences in a low voice and kept asking whether he had finished. She needed a {{e_secretletters|Secret love letters}} sent at once. The other man in the shadows mistook her proximity for something permitted only between lovers.

He turned his face to the wall. The actress took the paper, pushed a {{e_coin|Coins}} across the table and departed with her black lace and hurried whispers. When the door shut, the copyist sat down, elbows on his knees and hands over his ears, admitting over and over to himself that he loved her.

Then he sensed another silence in the room. It was as though his brother had already gone far away and was repeatedly saying goodbye. He could not understand why loving one person should cause another such pain. Still less could he understand whether a single decision could truly end it.

Candlelight fell upon two identical faces without revealing a common thought. The money remained on the table. Already the man beside the bed was eager to prove that he still placed his brother before everything else. He blew out the candle, lay down and announced, with excessive casualness, that he would never write for that woman again.

cards.title: The Door in the Rain

segments.text: After announcing that he would write no more letters, [[NPC1]] began his evening prayers, hoping the matter would pass. [[NPC2]] got up, lit the candle again and fastened his belt.
What is it?
I am going for a walk. You need not say those things for my sake. I do not care whether you write her letters.
Go back to bed. Who said it was for you? I do not want to write those letters for {{e_camila|Camila}} or take her money that way.
You love her. You need not change because of me.
Love her? What chance have I? If there were any chance, would she ask me to write these letters? Would she push a coin across the table every time?

The man at the table did not answer. His fingers tapped its edge. From the bed, his brother switched into their childhood {{e_language|The twins’ private language}}. The anger in his voice was more real, though even he did not wish to admit what lay within it.
I am perfectly well. Go to sleep. Do not be foolish.
No. I am going for a walk.
It is two o'clock and raining. You cannot walk about for hours like that. I promise you it is over. I only liked her for a little while.
[[NPC2]] stood in the doorway, his face almost taken by the dark.
I am in your way.
[[NPC1]] sprang from the bed. That sentence sounded less like an ordinary walk than a departure forever.
For God's sake, come back. Please come back.

His brother returned and lay down. When the actress's messenger came the next day, he received a definite refusal. For many days the brothers did not discuss the quarrel. Their silence did not mean that they understood one another entirely. The candle went out again. The door was shut. Outside, the rain continued.

cards.title: Every Hour

segments.text: [[NPC1]] cut his knee on a piece of metal. They had never known such illness. At first they merely watched the leg swell and the pain pass through his body in waves. At midnight they remembered a barber's sign advertising surgery. [[NPC2]] ran to knock at his door. The man had not returned; they must wait until morning.

They assured each other that all would be well once he had been seen. A day or two—perhaps less than a day—and the injured man would be out again. At last came {{e_medicine|Medicines and salves}} and plasters, with one clear instruction: apply cold wet cloths to the leg every hour.

The carer obeyed, but the patient grew worse. Each application of the {{e_cloth|Cold wet cloth}} brought the most unbearable moment. He begged his brother to stop, saying the pain had gone and there was no need. Afraid that yielding would delay recovery, the other lifted the covers and pressed the cloth firmly into place. The city's clocks struck the hours so sweetly outside. Inside, the sound became more dreadful.

Fever and pain disordered his mind. He cursed his brother and spoke of {{e_camila|Camila}}, as though everything he had been entitled to possess had been taken from him. His carer retreated outside and leaned against the door, struggling to breathe in his shock. After a while he still had to go in and perform the next duty.

Neighbours knocked on the wall; the landlord threatened to turn them out. He went out with a candle, endured their reproaches, then returned to the bedside. There was no new remedy, only another approaching hour. The instructions that had promised a quick recovery became something he dared not abandon and could no longer believe. Both still hoped that perhaps the next application would begin to make things better.

cards.title: A Lucid Moment

segments.text: I am better. The cloths must be helping after all. Tomorrow I shall be up, and you can sleep. I shall stop troubling you.
You are no trouble.
Towards dawn [[NPC1]] grew quiet. [[NPC2]] sat beside him. Several times words reached his lips before he finally spoke.
Shall I ask {{e_camila|Camila}} to visit? Even for a little while? Do you still think I stand between you? I told you I would not prevent anything.
Why mention her again? She means nothing to me. I am content as I am.
But you were so angry just now. When I put on the cloths, you were angry about that too. You cursed me…
My leg hurt. I did not know what I was saying. You are all I have. How could I curse you like that? You have gone too long without sleep. I have made you ill as well.
Morning light strengthened beyond the door. The {{e_cloth|Cold wet cloth}} still lay on the rim of the basin.
Let us miss this time. Once cannot matter. Perhaps it would be better to leave it quiet.
No. I have to get well. Give me the {{e_crucifix|Crucifix}}. If I say anything to hurt you again, I do not mean it. The pain makes me talk wildly. There, put it back. I am ready.
Truly, let us miss this one.
The doctor said we must do it. I shall not say another word.

Then it all began again. A promise made in clarity did not lessen the next agony. On the third night they sent for a priest. Amid the great wavering shadows, the man in the bed received the sacrament and died. No wet cloth had to be changed at the next exact hour. The watcher remained where he was, unable for a while to imagine what he should do first when daylight came.

cards.title: Across a Street

segments.text: After {{e_manuel|Manuel}} died, [[NPC1]] would not approach the building again. He walked for long hours, took detours, then drifted back to wander two streets away. The landlord could not arrange everything. He sent for the woman who had raised the brothers.
[[NPC2]] came, gave clear and practical instructions, then went to the corner. He watched her with both longing and suspicion. As she drew near, he turned his body and averted his face.
Will you help me a little? Come in and see your brother. Stay with me a while.
No.

She remembered the boys sitting at her knee while she told the story of the crucifixion. One had suddenly declared that, had they been there, they would have prevented it. Now this young man could not cross a familiar threshold. She did not reproach him. She changed the question and asked which brother he was.
Manuel.

Using the name he gave, she continued asking him to come inside. She recalled his errands for her and the soup he had brought when she was ill, without listing her own kindnesses to him. When at last she spoke of her own losses and of God's ordering of things, the young man slowly walked away. Twenty paces later he stopped again.

On the day of the funeral, candles burned even in daylight. Figures in black hoods sang a fearful hymn. He did not join the procession. He followed along parallel streets, reaching a crossing, glimpsing the line of people, then losing sight of it again.

cards.title: A Borrowed Answer

segments.text: She asked which one I was. I said {{e_manuel|Manuel}}. People always confused us before, and we did not always correct them. So long as the other was there, whether we corrected the same mistake hardly seemed to matter.

{{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} called that name and asked me inside. She did not say my answer was wrong. She only said she needed my help. I heard her mention the soup, the roads we used to take on errands. I remembered everything. Why had this short distance she wanted me to walk become so far?

I do not want to return to the {{e_room|Twins’ room}}, yet my walking always brings me near it. Around this street, then another, as though I am still on an unfinished errand. People pass me. None of them has to learn their old roads over again.

She said that she had lost someone too. I wanted to listen, and feared that next she would tell me how it ought to pass. So I walked away, then stopped and looked back. Someone behind me called. I did not know which name to return under.

cards.title: My Friend

segments.text: For months, reports of the young man came from everywhere. Someone had seen him in a dry riverbed, someone among ancient ruins; a shepherd found him standing on a mountain, wet with dew. He took work driving carts or tending sheep, stayed a while, then left without a word. He travelled far, but always returned to Lima.

A nun ran to tell [[NPC1]] that [[NPC2]] was outside again. She had imagined many ways to meet him: how could someone who had lost his brother be brought to live among people again? Now she suppressed her urgency and went to the door as calmly as she could.
My friend.
He stood trembling. She had seen the longing and distrust in those eyes before. She did not immediately ask for help or summon him inside. She merely repeated softly:
My friend.

She took a step forward. He suddenly turned and ran. Stumbling back to her desk, she knelt and angrily questioned God. She had prayed continually for wisdom; why had she received none? She was nothing but a scrubber of floors.

She punished herself for these words, but the punishment did not remove the problem before her. During that time she thought of {{e_captain|Captain Alvarado}}. Three weeks later they spoke for ten minutes. The following day he went in search of the young man, said to be copying for the university in Cuzco. One failed attempt to hold him had finally become a request for another person's help.

cards.title: The Dressing-Room Door

segments.text: I have climbed these backstage stairs so often, carrying copied {{e_scripts|Copied plays}} up and coming down again. I used to think only of finishing the errand and leaving. Now at the door, with nothing in my hands, I cannot explain why I have come.

{{e_camila|Camila}} sees me. I want badly to speak, but what should I say? That I am not the man who wrote her letters? Or that he can never come again? Once she drew us side by side and confidently declared one of us the younger. With only one face left, will she be more likely to mistake it?

There is a mirror and there are things for the stage. I remember that midnight when she leaned close to {{e_manuel|Manuel}}'s ear. From the bed I thought there was no place left for me. Later the place became empty again. Nothing returned to what it had been.
She waits. I look at her and still cannot find the sentence. The stairs are behind me. I go down them again. This time no one will ask why delivering a piece of work took so long.

cards.title: An Invitation to Supper

segments.text: [[NPC1]] entered the dim kitchen without greeting the young man at once. [[NPC2]] moved his chair farther into shadow. They had unloaded ships together before; none of the three had liked idle talk. The sailor's arrival pleased him a little and made him want to hide. Only when the meal was finished did the older man approach.
You have unloaded ships for me. I need strong men for my next voyage. Will you come? England, and Russia. Hard work, good pay, a long way from Peru.
The young man stared at the table and did not answer for a long while. The captain repeated the question.
Yes. I will go.
Good. Naturally I would like your brother to come too.
No.
Does he not want to? Let me talk to him. Where is he?
…Dead.
Both looked at the floor. When the captain asked his name, he gave his own this time. He did not borrow the other one.
When did {{e_manuel|Manuel}} die?
A few weeks ago. He hurt his knee. Only a few weeks.
How old are you?
Twenty-two. I must go. I have something to do in town.
Then come back this evening. Have supper with me and we will discuss the voyage. Come and have a little wine, will you?
Yes.
Neither found a sentence that could explain death. What remained at the table was simply a promise that could be kept: tonight, come back and sit here a while.

cards.title: Give Me Work

segments.text: Keep giving me work aboard, {{e_captain|Captain Alvarado}}. Anything. If the day is not enough, the night will do; I do not sleep well anyway. Do not leave me sitting there, waiting for the next bell.

And do not tell the others about me. I know they may mean well. But when they fall silent and look at me, I do not know how to stand. Pretend you never knew me. Give me the most work. Do not make me feel I am the one being specially watched.

I cannot copy at the desk anymore. The {{e_scripts|Copied plays}} lie before me, their words all neatly arranged, and still it seems another pen ought to be beside mine. Sometimes I would rather be too tired to think.

You asked about a man I once rescued. I remember that, and why I suddenly changed the subject while speaking of it. We once had a dog—no, not that now. Do you know {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}}? There is something I want to do for her before we leave.

cards.title: Not Mine Alone

segments.text: Before leaving I want to give {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} a {{e_gift|Gift for the abbess}}. Could I have my wages in advance? I shall not need money away. I want to buy it now.
Certainly. We will choose something in the morning.
It would not be from me alone. Once she… she once…

[[NPC1]] tried to speak his brother's name and could not. More quietly he mentioned that the abbess herself had told him of a terrible loss. He did not know whom she had lost, but had remembered her words.
I want to give her something. A thing like that is hard for her to bear.

He spoke for a long time. [[NPC2]] listened and promised to see to it the next day. When the young man fell forward in drunkenness, the captain went into the square outside the inn and looked at the mountains and clusters of stars. He too remembered a voice: do not be away too long; I shall be a big girl when you return.

His daughter was dead. {{e_maria|María}} had once heard him speak of her and put the story into a letter to her own daughter. Sometimes, he said, he felt the child was merely travelling—perhaps in England—and that he might see her again after a little while. No voyage, however far, had entirely left that illusion behind.

The captain went indoors, carried the young man to his room and sat watching him for a long time. Tomorrow's present still had no name. The person who had promised to arrange it was already here. The gift would belong to both brothers. For now, care had to begin with one living person.

cards.title: Hesitation on the Stairs

segments.text: Morning has come in {{e_cuzco|Cuzco}}. Yesterday I agreed. Standing on the stairs today, I discover that agreeing did not finish the matter. {{e_captain|Captain Alvarado}} waits below. Suddenly I say that I cannot go, cannot leave Peru after all.

He does not raise his voice. He asks about the present for {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}}. That was real; I do not want to take it back. She said she too had lost someone. I remember. Last night I tried to add another name to the gift and could not make my mouth say it.

Usually {{e_manuel|Manuel}} decided. Another job, another place: we could always go together. This time wherever I go, there will be only one person's footsteps. If I stay, the familiar roads have not changed either.

The captain says there will be work at sea. I need only fetch my things. I turn upstairs and walk that short distance very slowly. There is still someone outside waiting for me. I know he is there. I still do not know how to bring myself back to him.

cards.cgPrompt: A young man pauses halfway down a rough wooden inn staircase at morning, one hand on the banister, an older captain waiting below near the open doorway, bright mountain air outside contrasting with interior shadow.

cards.title: The Door Opens

segments.text: [[NPC1]] waited downstairs for a long time. He climbed part of the staircase and stopped to listen. At first there was no sound. Then a movement within told him that the young man was in danger.

He had known unbearable moments himself. For an instant he could not tell whether intervening would help. The hesitation lasted only a moment. He rushed upstairs, pushed open the door and caught hold of [[NPC2]], stopping what was happening.
Go away. Leave me alone. Do not come in now.

The young man sank to the floor, repeating that he was alone. The captain stood beside him, his face grey, his old suffering awakened. Knowing stars, currents and headlands did not mean he could find words of comfort. Away from matters of navigation, he had always spoken awkwardly.
We can only try. Try to go on. Time keeps passing. One day we shall be astonished that it has passed.

He did not know whether his words had been heard, and did not offer them as a guarantee. The young man did not rise at once. Someone speaking did not suddenly restore the whole meaning of life. There was simply another person in the room who was willing to stay.

The promised {{e_gift|Gift for the abbess}}, the harbour and the next voyage were all waiting beyond the door. For now the captain did not urge him downstairs. He gave the morning to something smaller and nearer: remaining with him through this moment.

cards.cgPrompt: A weathered captain has entered a modest inn bedroom and kneels near a grieving young man collapsed safely on the floor, the door open to morning light, expressive hands at rest, no rope, weapon, wound or self-harm method visible.

cards.title: On the Bridge, by the River

segments.text: We set out. The roads are still the same roads: one stretch, then another. I have not suddenly become someone else. I have not left last night in a closed room. Someone is merely walking beside me, without requiring an explanation for every step I am willing to take.

At the {{e_bridge|Bridge of San Luis Rey}}, {{e_captain|Captain Alvarado}} goes down to oversee the cargo crossing the river. It cannot go over this narrow footbridge; someone must attend to it by the water. I take the bridge. He goes about his work. We are supposed to meet again.
The young man stepped onto the bridge. Below, the business of moving cargo continued; above, footsteps fell upon the thin boards. During this crossing the bridge broke. He fell with it.

The captain remained below because of his work, not because he knew of any danger. There was no ceremony of farewell that day. Two people simply took two ordinarily unremarkable routes. Afterwards, when their voyage was mentioned, many sentences could go no farther than 'we were going to'.

cards.title: Always Through the Back Door

segments.text: At ten, [[NPC1]] ran from his father's estate to Madrid. His family made little effort to retrieve him. He handed out merchants' notices, watched horses and ran errands best left unexplained. Later he trained animals for travelling circuses, cooked and gathered information. He had his own ways of learning names, recognising faces and speaking to strangers.

Just as a business began to promise a fortune, he would often tire of it. He did not want possessions or lasting commitments to bind him, and above all did not want to be shut away. He could move from theatre to court, from antiques to silk, provided that next week he need not continue playing last week's man.

Eventually he came to Peru. In a few months he knew many people in the city, then connected reports from coastal towns, mines and the interior. {{e_viceroy|Viceroy Andrés}} discovered his usefulness. He passed along inconspicuous corridors, entered from behind, shared his patron's morning chocolate, and performed tasks unsuitable for ordinary attendants.

He could not understand why someone with such power took no greater pleasure in arranging other people's fates. But the man could quote Cervantes at will and knew which errands not to press upon him. That made the acquaintance worth keeping.

The city called him Uncle, without any definite kinship. He wrote letters for women, lent them money in distress, and stayed through illnesses longer than lovers or maids. Their lives offered places where he could come and go. He liked being trusted. He also liked knowing more than other people.
