cards.title: A House of Clever Animals

segments.text: Few people know I have a house. The dogs live downstairs, the birds above. Some of the dogs can do arithmetic. When I ask for a performance, they look at me earnestly. They are the ones waiting to hear me speak at home.

Money is not difficult to earn. The difficulty is having to stay too long in one place in order to keep a thing. I like coming and going freely, knowing who waits behind a door, knowing what someone wishes to ask before they speak.

Many people in {{e_lima|Lima}} call themselves cultivated. They pass the finest sentences in {{e_scripts|Copied plays}} as if passing an empty table. Change the order of a few words and the whole state of mind changes; they cannot even see it. I found these books little by little, borrowed some and stole others. I do not love them less because no one notices.

I have always wanted to write poetry. I have also wanted to find someone who could speak those sentences exactly as they should be spoken. When she began, I would no longer need to stand at the door explaining. Her voice itself would make people understand.

cards.cgPrompt: A thin middle-aged man with sparse beard alone in a modest house full of trained dogs, a caged songbird near an upper landing, an open Spanish playbook resting on his knee, late afternoon, affectionate yet solitary.

cards.title: A Song in the Café

segments.text: At twelve, [[NPC2]] was already singing in cafés. Her figure was still unformed, her face hungry and awkward, yet she could imitate every inflection of the mature singers before her. Sitting among the guitarists, [[NPC1]] listened and formed a resolution: he would cultivate this talent himself.

He paid to take the girl away. Instead of sleeping locked in the wine-storage room, she had a small bed in his house. There was hot soup, no whipping, and an opportunity to learn. These immediate changes were more real to her than the prospect of becoming a great artist.

He wrote songs, bought her new clothes and taught her to judge the quality of her voice. She practised acting, imitation and the creation of a whole song's atmosphere through sound. He took her to the {{e_theatre|Lima’s theatre}} and required her to notice every gesture. Hard-working, quiet and attentive, she learned faster than his boldest hopes.

She gradually became graceful and deeply loyal to her teacher. A trace of tension still crossed her face when he came too close. He noticed and maintained the distance. She sought his advice and trusted him to arrange their next journey. Clothing, meals, training and the next place to sing all entered her life through his hands.

In time her name would be known throughout the city. What he first saw was a child still imitating others. What she first received was not applause, but hot soup one evening, a bed no longer locked away, and the means to keep learning the next day. The man who paid also determined when and where she would next sing.

cards.cgPrompt: In a small colonial Lima cafe a lanky twelve-year-old girl in a worn plain dress sings beside seated guitarists while a thin older man with sparse moustache watches intently from the audience, modest tavern daylight, no glamour or adult styling.

cards.title: The Same Shawl

segments.text: Cafés like fresh faces. However well {{e_camila|Camila}} sang, after too long in one place we had to find another. So we travelled, our clothes wrapped together in the same {{e_shawl|Shawl}}. We slept in beds when there were beds, and on beaches when there were none.

We went to Mexico, were beaten in Panama and shipwrecked on a small Pacific island. There were snakes and beetles in the forest; one had to walk carefully. At harvest we hired our hands and legs to farmers. Many things cease to astonish once you have lived through them.

She was no child merely waiting to be looked after. Let her hear a song and she remembered its smallest turns. Let her watch a performance and she could say what had changed. The thought of such ability still growing made the next journey worth taking.

Later, people in {{e_lima|Lima}} saw only her fine clothes and heard her most accomplished voice. Sometimes I wanted to tell them that once all we owned fitted into a shawl. If she did not wish to mention it onstage, I listened below. On those roads, she too gave me a reason to continue. I simply kept believing that I knew better where the future ought to lead. When the rain stopped, we had to travel on.

cards.cgPrompt: An older travelling tutor and a young adolescent singer rest on a Pacific beach beside a single bundled shawl containing their clothes, simple worn footwear, distant small boats, pale dawn, companions enduring an ordinary difficult journey.

cards.title: After the Applause

segments.text: Returning to her dressing room, [[NPC1]] heard the whistling in the corner and knew that something had been wrong again tonight. [[NPC2]] said it was nothing; she had done her best. That tone was harder to bear than an accusation, as though her talent could go no farther.
What was it? What now? I am ready to hear it. Do not stand there like that.
Nothing, my little pearl.
I know there were weak moments tonight. You need not tell me. I only wanted to come back here without seeing you look like that.
Why did you speak so quickly to the prisoner?

One day you want it faster, another slower. The audience has never given such {{e_applause|Applause}}. They wept. That is all I care about. Stop talking. You may comb my hair, if you do not say another word.
For ten minutes he combed her hair as if he did not see her shaking with tears. At last she turned and seized his hand.
Was I so bad? Bad enough to make you leave your seat?
The scene on the ship was good. The ending was quite good too. But the speech to the prisoner…

She buried her face in her arms on the table. Only perfection would suffice, and perfection never truly arrived. When the sobbing subsided, they spoke again of voice, gesture and pace, repeating lines from the {{e_scripts|Copied plays}}. The audience had long been satisfied. They often continued until dawn, approaching a standard neither could quite deliver.

cards.cgPrompt: A brilliant actress exhausted after a performance sits at a cluttered dressing table while her thin older tutor stands in the corner withholding praise, a comb and pomade jars, tears in her expression, warm backstage candlelight, no glamour portrait.

cards.title: The Poet's Granddaughter

segments.text: I told {{e_camila|Camila}} that the poet's granddaughter had come. We chose one of his {{e_scripts|Copied plays}} and rehearsed it again and again. She had grown tired of roles that revolved endlessly around men. This time every sentence commanded her attention anew.

Before the performance she peered through the curtain and asked me to point out the visitor. I indicated a middle-aged woman worn down by housekeeping, children and poverty. She looked as though she had seen all the nobility in the world, standing beside me without a word.

Afterwards I led the visitor into the dressing room. Weeping, she knelt to kiss the woman's hands; the woman kissed hers in return. The audience went home. The lamps remained lit. They were still talking about how the poet wrote, and the small habits at home that strangers never knew.

That night I demanded nothing more. She had brought what I treasured most onto the stage, and received from a stranger an answer that was not merely for her beauty. The joy remained after the applause had faded.

cards.cgPrompt: An older theatre tutor at the edge of a dressing room watches his young adult actress kneel to greet a modest middle-aged visitor, costumes hanging on the wall, exhausted joy after a performance, the visitor clasping her hands in return.

cards.title: A Supper Reaching Dawn

segments.text: By the time [[NPC1]] arrived after a performance, it was often one in the morning. Her jewels dazzled; she was exhausted. [[NPC2]] and his guests welcomed her like a queen. At first she led the conversation and laughter. Gradually she leaned against her host's shoulder, listening as the talk passed from one interesting, ageing face to another.

{{e_pio|Pio}} was there, with the literary {{e_archbishop|Archbishop of Lima}} in violet and the widely travelled {{e_captain|Captain Alvarado}}. They discussed wars, kings, poets and distant countries; ghosts, whether a departing soul could be seen, whether stars might collide. As the night deepened, each found it easier to turn a regret into a witty story.

They all missed {{e_spain|Spain}}, and assured themselves that this conversation embodied the noble Spanish spirit. The actress learned a new ease from such life: how to hold a glass casually, take leave at a door, or speak a title as though she had known it from childhood. Pio noticed these details in her performances and felt they added lustre.

At last golden morning light crossed the Andes and reached the fruit, the wine-stained cloth and her sleeping forehead. The talk ceased. No one wished to rise first. Their eyes rested on her as on a beautiful bird that had accidentally flown into the room.

She believed she would be happy forever. Her teacher continued to observe, waiting for experience to deepen enough to improve certain speeches. The supper brought each a little comfort. They had never wanted the same thing from this woman. Outside, the city woke. At the table they delayed the moment with old stories.

cards.cgPrompt: Dawn entering a colonial palace supper room where a tired actress sleeps leaning against the viceroy's sleeve, an archbishop in violet, a thin theatre tutor and weathered sea captain sit quietly around fruit and brocade, intimate faded grandeur, not a banquet crowd.

cards.title: The Face After the Performance

segments.text: Once my face is still, the person in the mirror is not the one the audience saw. The mouth looks tired; the eyes seem always to be searching. I can learn the smile a role requires. After the performance I do not know whom to give it to.

{{e_viceroy|Viceroy Andrés}} teaches me French and the manners of important people when they are not receiving formal guests. I learn quickly. Onstage, the way my fingers touch a glass or I pause before a doorway delights even {{e_pio|Pio}}. When my life enters a play, he thinks everything has been useful.

But I do not live only for the next performance. {{e_applause|Applause}} sometimes warms me. Sometimes it resembles an account settled punctually each day. The audience does not notice when my mind wanders. My teacher does, and feels that I have failed something again.

I want to fall in love, to have a home, to sit quietly when no one is inspecting me. Each wish takes up space. Yet every day this same body must dress, learn lines, make its entrance and hurry smiling to another late supper.

cards.cgPrompt: An adult actress alone before a plain dressing mirror after removing part of her stage costume, long fine nose, tired slightly childish mouth, dark reflective eyes, jewelry set aside, natural morning light revealing fatigue rather than ugliness.

cards.title: A Respectable Form of Address

segments.text: At about thirty, [[NPC1]] left the stage. It took another five years to establish herself in society. Accompanied by women friends and servants, she attended church at fashionable hours, appeared at university ceremonies and joined lists of charitable donors. She called her old performances a diversion, as though they were a past into which one ought not enquire too seriously.

She learned a little reading and writing, arranged respectable relations for herself and secured legitimacy for her children. Any hint that someone considered her a wandering entertainer brought a fierce response. She wanted more than fine clothes: she wanted respect that her origins could not casually take away.

But {{e_respectability|Respectability}} did not readily produce the peace she had imagined. She strove to be gentle before great ladies, and became more irritable elsewhere. Ornaments and feathers accumulated. In mirrors and polished floors she increasingly resembled a woman who had arrived. She herself still waited for the happiness her position had promised.

Gradually she hinted that {{e_pio|Pio}} should avoid her in public. Later even his private visits irritated her. Polite phrases, averted eyes and quarrels always ready to begin separated her old companion from her new life.

He still came once a month. When conversation failed, he went upstairs to see the children. Both adults remembered how they had once lived together. One was eager to prove she could change; the other kept hoping that their old intimacy might return unchanged.

cards.cgPrompt: A former actress dressed as a respectable colonial lady enters a university ceremony with attendants, elaborate but slightly excessive jewels and scarf, her guarded expression distinct from the pleased onlookers, restrained literary period illustration.

cards.title: A Child in the Sunshine

segments.text: {{e_jaime|Jaime}} walks a few paces behind. The ladies who try to detain him in conversation make him uneasy. He earnestly finds a way to escape them, then follows again. In fine weather we walk like this among the terraces of the {{e_garden|French garden}}, saying little.

In his garnet velvet he was so small and so solemn. During an attack, it seemed the hardest part was not his own suffering but having others see it. He inherited my forehead and eyes, and his father's bodily frailty. I cannot bear even a moment of it for him.

I wait for life to satisfy me at last. He is pleased simply because the sun is out. He watches a cloud as if calculating when it will cover us. I do not lose my temper with him, nor am I given to suddenly taking him in my arms. We keep those few paces between us and continue.

The place has been made to resemble Europe: carefully arranged trees, railings and paths. Everyone knows the proper manner of strolling. Among them this child and I sometimes seem like foreigners who have not learned the language. After a spell of illness, he still tries to keep a little farther from the solicitous ladies.

cards.cgPrompt: A stately woman and a delicate seven-year-old boy in garnet velvet walk several paces apart on artificial French garden terraces in the Andes, the child quietly enjoying a patch of sunlight, she preoccupied, gentle dignified portrayal of illness.

cards.title: An Island That Did Not Exist

segments.text: At dusk [[NPC1]] waited beside a chipped marble bench. He hoped to recover the trust and jokes of their wandering years. When [[NPC2]] arrived, she first corrected his familiar form of address, then impatiently told him to call her what he liked.
If you want me back at the {{e_theatre|Lima’s theatre}}, say no more. The thought of that place frightens me. So many insults every day. Enough.
If you were happy with these new friends, I would not ask you to return.
You dislike my friends? Whom do you propose to replace them with? I want no advice. Forget me.
He did not understand why she wept and continued describing the theatre's decline. Suddenly she touched his knee, looking as she had many years before.

Forgive me. {{e_jaime|Jaime}} was ill again this afternoon. He lay there so white, so astonished, and no one could help. One has to think of other things. But returning to act would be useless. The audience wants new farces. There is no point fighting it.
I was unjust. I was proud and withheld the praise you deserved. You were always a great actress. We could still go to {{e_spain|Spain}}. You would succeed in Madrid.
The world is the same everywhere.
Or to an island, where people would love you for yourself.
Fifty years old, and still dreaming of such islands. They exist only in plays.

At last she said she was cold and must go. Unable to find words true enough for parting, she bent and kissed his fingers. He remained alone in the thickening cloud, pleased by the gesture and still trying to understand what the conversation had given him.

cards.cgPrompt: At dusk a thin fifty-year-old man sits beside a chipped marble garden bench while a former actress stands nearby in a dark shawl, Andes behind a balustrade, first clouds entering the terrace, poignant distance between old companions.

cards.title: The Children Upstairs

segments.text: I have come again this month. {{e_camila|Camila}}'s politeness grows more complete, so complete that no answer is possible. She does not meet my eyes. I look at the furnishings, thinking that if I stay a little longer, perhaps we will speak of something from the past.

When conversation fails, I go upstairs to the children. {{e_jaime|Jaime}} is there too. They do not yet require me to change my identity at the door, or prove that my clothes and reputation belong in this house. I stay with them, meet a small need, and the remaining time passes upstairs. At least I can still offer this {{e_care|Care}}.

On my way back to {{e_lima|Lima}}, people embrace in the streets and take smiling leave of one another. Surely, I think, they draw great comfort from these meetings. We once had that too, without formality or an appointed ten minutes: walking long roads together, speaking whenever something happened.

I know she has her own life now. Still, I hope that next time she calls me Uncle, her voice might sound a little as it used to. Such a small wish keeps me thinking of next month's visit all the way home. If the children still listen, the long journey seems not entirely wasted.

cards.cgPrompt: An older thin tutor sits quietly with three children in an upstairs room while the formal drawing room below is left empty, one delicate boy listening closest, simple books on a table, afternoon gentleness and loneliness.

cards.title: The Gifts Returned

segments.text: News of the smallpox spread through Lima. Hundreds of others were ill, yet the talk and malice gathered around [[NPC1]]. Many secretly hoped that the beauty which had enabled her to leave her former class would finally be damaged. Each rumour from the sickroom seemed to compensate those who rejoiced in her misfortune.

As soon as she could travel, she left the city for the mountains. She would sell the fine house and gowns, return the {{e_jewels|Jewels}} to their donors. {{e_viceroy|Viceroy Andrés}}, the {{e_archbishop|Archbishop of Lima}} and people who had sincerely liked her still sent enquiries and presents. The messages went unanswered. The presents came back unopened.

She allowed no one but her nurse and maid to see her. After so many years of admiration, she had bound other people's desire for her company to her face. If they still came now, it must be pity; hidden within their pity, she imagined satisfaction at the reversal.

She returned more money than she owed. When her anger eased, poverty began to approach. The farm declined. Her children were still there, but her days narrowed to a room she would not leave. She imagined the city's delight and, hearing a footstep, could not tell whether it brought help or another examining gaze.

{{e_pio|Pio}} did not give up. He watched the children, helped manage the farm and quietly lent her money, eventually gaining admission again. She received him veiled, still speaking sharply. He believed he understood her suffering. Understanding did not mean that every door in the house was therefore open to him.

cards.cgPrompt: A veiled former actress in a shuttered country villa returns jewelry and letters to a closed box beside the door, a nurse in the background, diffused daylight, privacy and exhaustion, illness never shown as grotesque spectacle.

cards.title: No Visitors

segments.text: Do not bring those things in again. Send them back. Tell them there is no need to enquire. Once I accepted a string of beads and thought it affection. Now the same box on the table makes me wonder only whether its sender has heard about my face.

This {{e_villa|Camila’s villa}} once seemed a respectable destination. Now every person waiting outside my room makes me want to shut the door more tightly. Perhaps {{e_pio|Pio}} does not think that way. Perhaps he truly means to help. The moment he looks at me, I have already supplied his thoughts.

I returned the presents, even those I did not have to return. At least I would no longer owe anyone the right to look at me. Only later did I notice how little money remained. A farm does not recover by itself because a door is closed.

The children are upstairs. {{e_jaime|Jaime}} has always been so frail. I ought to find some help for him, yet every day I have less strength even to leave this room. I refuse pity. I do not know another way to speak my need.

cards.cgPrompt: A woman in a plain dark veil seated beside closed shutters in a country villa, one hand on an unanswered letter, face partly visible with subtle healed smallpox marks but no exaggeration, soft cool interior light and dignified framing.

cards.title: A Visitor in the Mirror

segments.text: [[NPC1]] believed she had locked the door. For a brief moment a secret hope returned: after all the methods she had learned onstage, might there be one that could restore something familiar to her face?

She mixed powder with cream and applied it hurriedly. Once she had laughed at old women at court with faces painted white. Now she faced the {{e_mirror|Dressing mirror}}, anxious and unwilling to admit that her hope was failing. The colour did not restore the past. It only made her more aware of what she had done.

Then she saw [[NPC2]] reflected at the door. He had pushed it open and stood there in surprise. She sprang up, covered her face with both hands and screamed. What was unbearable was not simply that he had seen the marks of illness. He had seen her secret wish to conceal them.
Get out. Never enter my house again. I do not want to see you.

She followed him into the corridor, hurled things down the stairs and ordered the steward never to admit him to the grounds. The prohibition was clear. For another week he repeatedly tried to see her, then temporarily returned to {{e_lima|Lima}}.

He could manage accounts, lend money and secure care for the children. He had failed to pause and ask before opening a door. The woman faced the mirror alone again. This time, besides a little secret hope, she had lost the certainty that her door was locked.

cards.cgPrompt: A woman applying a simple pale cosmetic mixture in private sees an older tutor reflected unexpectedly at her open doorway; she lifts her hands to cover her face, framed from behind and side with a mirror, dignified distress, no grotesque makeup or voyeuristic close-up.

cards.title: Another Mountain Journey

segments.text: Back in {{e_lima|Lima}}, I found tasks to fill the time. None held me long. Longing makes a fool of a man. At my age I was still like an eighteen-year-old, thinking that one more meeting might allow everything to be explained.

{{e_camila|Camila}} had forbidden me to enter the grounds. If I knocked as usual, I knew my words would never reach her. I began to devise another way, a voice that would make her come outside herself. I had used ingenuity to enter many doors before. This time I refused to accept her refusal as final.

I thought of {{e_jaime|Jaime}} too. The child was intelligent and wanted to learn. He should not spend all day among servants and stables. I could teach him, put my house in order and ask {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} to find a housekeeper.

These plans all sounded useful. Thinking of them, I felt I had a reason to climb the mountain road once more. Before dawn, every shutter and door was closed. I stood outside, rehearsing inwardly the voice that did not belong to me.

cards.cgPrompt: A thin fifty-year-old man walks back toward a secluded Andean country villa before dawn with a small travel bag, dark shrub-lined path, a single shuttered window distant above him, anxious persistence rather than heroic resolve.

cards.title: Estrella

segments.text: [[NPC1]] lay beneath the window, imitating a girl's low sobs. He kept the sound quiet and intermittent for a full quarter of an hour. The faintest blue appeared behind the mountains; grass stirred in the breeze. At last a lamp lit upstairs, the shutter opened, and the veiled [[NPC2]] looked out.
Who is there? Who is crying?
Señora, please come down. I am a poor girl called Estrella. Do not send the maid. Come yourself and help me.
After a pause she agreed. A little later her heavy cloak trailed through the dewy grass. She came round the corner of the house, still keeping her distance.
Come here to me. Who are you?
The visitor stood and admitted who he was. The woman who had come to help an unknown girl understood at once that she had been lured outside.
When will I be rid of you? I want to see no one, speak to no one.
For the sake of all our years together, grant me one thing. I shall leave and trouble you no more.
I shall grant nothing. Stay away.
She went towards a door on the other side. He had to hurry after her to keep within hearing. At last she stopped, tired and angry.
What is it? Quickly. It is cold, and I am not well yet.

He asked to take {{e_jaime|Jaime}} to the city for a year and educate him himself. The morning star still shone above. The girl supposedly calling for help did not exist. The person truly drawn into this conversation was a child still asleep inside.

cards.cgPrompt: Before sunrise outside a country villa a veiled woman in a heavy cloak has come to help someone and discovers an older thin man rising from the shadow beneath her window, dew on grass and pale blue Andes, betrayal and distance, no frightened child present.

cards.title: Ask the Child First

segments.text: No. {{e_jaime|Jaime}} is frail, and your house is disorderly. Only the country suits him.
He has been better these past months. I shall put the house in order, ask {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} for a housekeeper and teach him Spanish, Latin, music, everything he ought to know. Only a year.
A mother cannot part with her child like that. The children and I will manage as best we can. Think no more about me.
When his request failed, [[NPC2]] abruptly changed his appeal.
Then repay the money you owe me.
[[NPC1]] stopped. The poverty she had laboured to conceal was laid bare before her. After a silence her voice became hoarse.

I have very little money. I shall give you what I have. There are a few {{e_jewels|Jewels}} left; you may have them now. Then we need never see one another again. So you are that hard-hearted. Still, I owe the money and ought to repay it.
I do not want the money. I only said it to make you grant my request. Let me educate him for a year. I shall love and care for him. Was I a bad teacher before?
Gratitude, gratitude, always gratitude. You are cruel. I was grateful once—very well. But I am no longer that woman.
She looked at the stars for a while without agreeing. When she spoke again, another person's wishes finally entered the conversation.
If the boy wishes to go with you, he may. I shall ask him in the morning. If he wishes it, you will find him at the inn at noon. Good night. God keep you.

She turned indoors. The demand for repayment had been withdrawn; it could not be treated as though it had never been made. The promise of education still awaited the child's waking answer. She had not surrendered a mother's right to decide forever.

cards.cgPrompt: A veiled mother and her older former tutor face each other outside a country house at dawn, she standing firmly near the doorway while he pleads with open hands, no child in frame, the cold blue light softening toward morning.

cards.title: We Shall Rest Across the Bridge

segments.text: At noon the next day, the solemn little boy arrived at the inn. His once fine clothes were worn and stained. He carried only a small bundle of changes. His mother had given him a gold {{e_coin|Coins}} for spending money and a {{e_stone|Little shining stone}} to look at in the dark when he could not sleep.

[[NPC1]] took [[NPC2]] into the cart. Before long he saw that the jolting made the child unwell. He lifted him onto his shoulders and continued. Languages, music and manners—the things he planned to teach—were still waiting in the city. First he must care for a body that could not endure the bouncing wheels.

Near the valley the boy felt a familiar attack approaching. He wanted to conceal his shame, especially before strangers. Just then they met {{e_captain|Captain Alvarado}}, an acquaintance of the older man. The adults' greetings were ordinary. The child attended only to keeping his face and hands carefully composed.

Farther on, the older man exchanged words with an elderly woman travelling with a girl: {{e_maria|María}} and {{e_pepita|Pepita}}. Each had arrived by a separate history. For a moment they became a company crossing a river.

He said they would sit down and rest across the bridge. The child did not have to finish the whole journey, only reach the other side. It was a plain, practical plan of care: find somewhere to sit, let this spell pass, then continue towards the city.

They did not reach that resting place. The bridge fell into the valley that day. Five lives, previously separate, would thereafter be spoken of under the same date. {{e_juniper|Brother Juniper}} witnessed the moment from before the bridge. Later he would ask whether it was chance or {{e_providence|Providence}}. {{e_letters|Letters between mother and daughter}}, memories and contradictory accounts would bring those names before him again.

cards.cgPrompt: A thin older man with sparse beard carries a delicate young boy on his shoulder as they approach a narrow Andean rope footbridge; boy holds a small bundle and looks tired, an older noblewoman and young girl ahead near the entrance, distant cargo path below, no falling or collapse.

cards.title: The Stone in the Luggage

segments.text: {{e_jaime|Jaime}} wishes to go. Now things must be prepared; they cannot remain inside last night's 'if'. The clothes are no longer as fine as before. {{e_pio|Pio}} will see, perhaps others in the city too. I cannot keep the child in this house merely to conceal that.

A gold {{e_coin|Coins}}, for him to spend himself. And this {{e_stone|Little shining stone}}: when he cannot sleep, he can look at it in the dark instead of staring only into blackness. I cannot give him a night without pain or fear. I can give him this small thing at hand.
We agreed on a year. I also remember the cruel words spoken this morning, and why I refuse another demand for gratitude. Entrusting my child to him has not erased those things.

There is little luggage. Once it is packed, the table is empty again. I remain in this {{e_villa|Camila’s villa}}; no one need keep waiting at the door. Yet when I think of him sleeping in another room tonight, I still want to touch the bundle I have already given away.

segments.text: María rose from a cloth merchant’s daughter to become the Marquesa de Montemayor. She resisted marriage, yet eventually entered the chapel amid the guests’ derision. Her daughter’s birth gave her one child on whom to lavish all the love she had never received. Clara grew up under that anxious attention, needing ever more distance. The more her mother feared rejection, the harder she tried to please and the more she talked. When Clara shut the door, María waited outside for an answer that would reassure her. She remembered the fears of her own childhood; that memory alone could not keep her from becoming a burden to another child.

pages.title: A letter cannot shorten the sea

segments.text: Clara chose a marriage that would take her to Spain. She boarded calmly, leaving her mother on the shore. Four years later, María was at last allowed to visit. Both resolved to change, and both wounded the other again. Before dawn María kissed her daughter’s door and returned to Peru. She entrusted to letters the feelings they could scarcely bear face to face. She collected jokes, read books and polished her sentences, hoping Clara would linger over them. Those letters survived, chiefly because her son-in-law preserved them. Their writer still wanted only a little closeness. Alone on her balcony, she also recognized the wish to control within her longing for an answer, but could not let it go.

pages.title: The child entrusted with a future

segments.text: Fearing that no one would continue her work, the abbess chose Pepita beside the laundry trough. She gave the girl difficult errands, taught her about wards and accounts, then sent her to the Marquesa’s house to learn about life beyond the convent. Pepita was proud to be trusted and afraid she was unequal to it. In her new home, bullying servants and the lady’s wavering affection left her no one she could safely confide in. Once the Marquesa told her to wait outside a church, then left by another door. Even after learning that she had gone, Pepita returned to the street corner to wait. She knew how to hold fast to a duty; she did not yet know how to ask for help with her own troubles.

At the theatre, Camila improvised a song mocking the Marquesa and won the audience’s applause. Pepita understood and led her mistress out. The Marquesa, absorbed in thoughts of her distant daughter, had scarcely heard. Sent by the Viceroy to apologize, the actress mistook her bewilderment for forgiveness and felt real shame. María described a tender reconciliation with Clara. It was only a dream she had had many times. When news of Clara’s pregnancy arrived, her mother sought help in prohibitions, charms and prayers, then took Pepita on a mountain pilgrimage. While her mistress hurried to the shrine, the girl stayed at the inn to arrange trunks, charcoal and food, making an unfamiliar room a place they could inhabit.

pages.title: What survived, what was torn up

segments.text: The clear mountain air briefly quieted María. Clara’s new letter still hurt, but she no longer rushed to seek a guarantee. Alone, Pepita wrote to ask for a few days back at the convent and a few words from the abbess. While the girl was downstairs, the Marquesa read her appeal. Before supper Pepita refused to send it, calling it insufficiently brave; later she tore it up. Her words made María reconsider her own demands. She wrote anew the letter later known as Letter LVI, calling it her first. As dawn approached she looked in on the sleeping girl. They set out for Lima two days later. The appeal for help did not survive; the mother’s new letter reached people who would live on.

pages.title: Two people who need no explanation

segments.text: Manuel and Esteban were found in a basket outside the convent and grew up under the abbess’s care. They heard many stories. As a boy, Manuel insisted that if the brothers had been present at the Crucifixion, they would have stopped it. Grown up, they copied texts, loaded cargo and took temporary jobs. Strangers’ jokes about their identical faces made them avoid appearing together in the street. They also had a private language invented in childhood. When the Archbishop wanted to record its words, that intimacy made them too embarrassed to speak. To others they seemed uncommunicative. Together they needed few words to know that someone was there.

One evening of free admission, Esteban left the theatre first; Manuel stayed to watch Camila dance. His attraction deepened. He agreed to write her secret love letters, telling even his brother nothing. Their declarations and anger were addressed to other men. One late night she came to their rented room to dictate. From his bed, Esteban mistook their close whispering for an intimacy he could not share. Seeing his brother’s pain, Manuel announced that he would stop writing for her. Esteban said there was no need to change on his account and even tried to leave in the rain. Both stayed. They did not return to the quarrel. Silence was restored, but the distance between them had not been fully explained.

pages.title: A wet cloth and one name

segments.text: Manuel injured his knee and grew steadily worse. The doctor ordered cold applications every hour. Esteban stayed to replace the wet cloths, only to find that these were his brother’s moments of greatest pain. Curses poured out in his illness and were retracted when he was lucid. Both kinds of words truly wounded the caregiver; they cannot simply be assembled into a final confession. Manuel died on the third night. The abbess came to arrange the burial. The survivor would not enter the building and even gave his dead brother’s name when asked who he was. As the funeral moved through the city, he followed along parallel streets, seeing it from a distance and losing it from a distance.

Esteban wandered for a long time, sometimes working, sometimes suddenly leaving. He went to Camila’s dressing room but could not speak. Outside the convent, the abbess twice called him her friend; he turned and ran. At last she thought of the Captain and asked him to find the young man in Cuzco. The Captain offered work and an invitation to supper. Here Esteban spoke his own name again. Over the meal he asked for constant work aboard ship and for no one to be told his history. The conversation did not lift his grief, but it left another meeting and a journey together still to come.

pages.title: They were meant to meet again

segments.text: Esteban wanted an advance on his wages to give the abbess a present from himself and his dead brother. What to buy had not yet been decided. The Captain agreed, recognizing in the young man his own grief for his daughter. The next day Esteban withdrew his promise and returned upstairs in crisis. The Captain entered and kept him among the living, without promising that a few words could make grief disappear. Later they set out together and separated at the bridge: the Captain went down into the gorge to supervise the cargo, while Esteban took the footbridge. They were meant to meet again. The bridge broke. Setting out had been an attempt to continue living; it brought no guarantee from fate.

Pio left home in childhood and made a living by his memory, connections and ingenuity. He loved freedom, beautiful women and Spanish literature. He knew many people’s secrets, yet often had only trained dogs and birds for company at home. He noticed twelve-year-old Camila singing in a café and paid to take her away. First came hot soup, a small bed and an end to beatings; strict training followed. They toured together with their clothes in one shawl, enduring poverty and danger. He watched her talent grow rapidly, while she found work she wanted to give herself to. Their closeness always coexisted with unequal power.

Even after the audience was satisfied, Camila had to face Pio’s whistling and criticism. The dressing room held tears and rehearsals that lasted until dawn. He could help her understand a detail, yet often drove her by withholding praise. On the night they performed for the poet’s granddaughter, they also shared a true artistic joy. Later, the Viceroy’s suppers brought manners, experience and status. Pio was pleased to see these improve her acting. Camila still had to bear the weariness of love, daily life and her body. The life she wanted was not solely in the service of the next speech.

Camila left the stage and spent years seeking respectability, making a new position for herself and her children. Walking through her mountain garden, she still waited for happiness to begin. Her frail son Jaime was glad simply to be in the sunshine. Pio visited monthly; after a cold reception he went upstairs to the children, still hoping their former closeness might return. In their dusk conversation in the garden, he belatedly admitted how little praise he had given her. He proposed Madrid or an island of his dreams. Camila refused to return to the theatre, then apologized after mentioning the child’s attack that afternoon. Finally she kissed his fingers. The gesture brought warmth without making their futures one again.

After smallpox, Camila returned gifts, moved to her villa and refused visitors. She understood their concern as pity tinged with superiority, gradually shutting out help as well. Pio cared for the children and managed the estate. At last allowed inside, he unexpectedly opened a door she believed locked. The mirror showed her secret attempt to powder her face, and the visitor’s surprise. Furious, she drove him out and forbade him even the courtyard. Back in Lima he could not rest. He climbed the road again, imagining that he might educate Jaime. His good intentions and his intrusions coexist; neither cancels the other.

Pio imitated a weeping girl to draw Camila outside, then asked to take Jaime to the city for a year’s education. Refused, he pressed her by demanding repayment of a debt, then withdrew the demand for money. Camila finally set a condition: first ask whether the child wished to go. Jaime appeared next day with a gold coin from his mother and a little stone to look at when sleepless. The jolting journey made him ill, so Pio carried him on his shoulder. Before the bridge they met the Captain and spoke to María and Pepita. Their plan to rest on the other side was never fulfilled. Education, homecoming and voyage all remained unfinished. Those who survived still had to live with love, wrongs and care.
